title: Heat flow did not clearly change 10-day aftershock counts after 601 onshore shallow Japanese mainshocks (Mj 3.5-7.3, 1999-2024); mainshock depth was the clearest control
abstract: A damage rheology model predicts fewer aftershocks in hot crust. We tested this prediction with the JMA catalog. We selected 934 independent onshore natural mainshocks (Mj 3.5-7.3, depth 25 km or less, 1999-2024). We counted aftershocks of M >= Mm-2 in 10 days. We used three thermal proxies: the median GHFDB heat flow within 30 km (601 mainshocks), the distance to the nearest Holocene volcano, and the local D90 depth. The negative binomial models control magnitude, depth and background rate. The intervals come from a bootstrap of 0.5-degree cells. Heat flow gave a factor of 1.06 per doubling (95% interval 0.86-1.30), and all 16 design changes included no change. Inside 2-degree regions, the factor was 0.81 (0.56-1.12). So the data do not exclude a moderate local decrease. Mainshocks nearer to volcanoes had more aftershocks (0.67 per tenfold distance, 0.49-0.91). This excess went near zero inside regions (0.91, 0.57-1.39) and became unclear without foreshock sequences. Foreshock counts also increased near volcanoes. Thus the excess agrees with swarm-like regional activity, not with a smooth thermal control. Mainshocks that were 10 km shallower had 1.79 times more aftershocks (1.40-2.32). D90 had a link only when we did not control mainshock depth. The aftershock b-values (0.79-0.88) and the share of late aftershocks did not change clearly with any proxy. Limitations: the heat-flow sites are sparse and of mixed quality, there are no focal mechanisms, Mj is not Mw, the mainshock rules are simple windows, and we did not correct for multiple tests.

display.caption: Observed divided by expected 10-day aftershock counts (M >= Mm-2) in quintiles of (a) local heat flow, (b) distance to the nearest Holocene volcano and (c) local D90 depth. Blue: the expected counts control magnitude, depth and background. Orange: the expected counts do not control depth. The bars show 95% cluster bootstrap intervals over 0.5-degree cells.

Productivity factors for each thermal proxy, for the primary design and 16 design changes. The data are negative binomial GLM coefficients with 95% cluster bootstrap intervals. The last row adds offshore and island events, where the detection threshold is not uniform; we do not interpret that row.

(a) GHFDB R2024 heat-flow sites (0 < q <= 250 mW/m2) and GVP Holocene volcanoes. (b) The 934 onshore shallow JMA mainshocks of 1999-2024, coloured by tercile of distance to the nearest volcano and sized by magnitude.

Found an inverse link between stacked aftershock productivity and heat flow in southern California. Our pooled Japanese result does not show a clear inverse link.
Found more swarm-like activity in high heat flow areas of southern California. Our excess of foreshocks and aftershocks near Japanese volcanoes agrees with swarm-like activity.
Enescu and Furuya found no significant heat-flow link for 18 Japanese sequences of Mj 5.5 or more. We test about 50 times more sequences and find no clear pooled link.
